title: Break it on purpose
goal: The most instructive twenty minutes in this project. Measure the failure before you fix it — otherwise resilience configuration is guesswork you cannot defend.
startWith: Step 05 finished: both services running, holds working.

newIdeas.plain: The response time that 99% of requests beat. Averages hide disasters: a service can average 40ms while one request in a hundred takes thirty seconds.

Account stops answering. Ledger's threads all sit waiting on it. Ledger runs out of threads and stops answering anything, including requests that never needed account. One sick service has taken down a healthy one.

A crashed dependency is easy: the connection is refused immediately. A hung one accepts your connection and never replies, so you wait forever. That is why you freeze the process rather than kill it in the test below.
The upper bound on how long you will wait. It is the cheapest and most valuable line of configuration here — everything else in this step is a refinement on top of it.

A counter around the call. Too many recent failures and it stops calling for a while, failing instantly instead. It protects the caller's threads, and gives the sick service room to recover instead of being hammered.
What you return when the call fails or is short-circuited. Degrading — a slightly stale balance view — usually beats an error page.

tasks.do: Install a load generator and record a baseline p99
tasks.why: Without a number from before the fix, you cannot tell whether the fix worked.
tasks.how: hey is the simplest option; k6 is nicer if you already have it. Run thirty seconds of load against the hold endpoint while both services are healthy, and write the p99 down somewhere you will still have it in ten minutes.

blocks.label: Install one of them
blocks.body:
go install github.com/rakyll/hey@latest      # anywhere with Go
# macOS:      brew install hey
# Windows:    winget install k6 --source winget   (then use k6 below)

blocks.label: Baseline: 30s of load, both services healthy

check.run: # write down the p99 from the latency distribution

tasks.do: Freeze account mid-test and watch ledger die with it
tasks.why: This is the failure every pattern in stages B, C and D is defending against. You should see it once, on your own machine.
tasks.how: Freeze rather than stop the process: SIGSTOP leaves the port open and answers nothing, which is far nastier than a crash and much more like a real overloaded service. Watch the live thread count climb while it is frozen — that is your thread pool filling with requests that will never complete.

blocks.label: Freeze account (Windows PowerShell, if lsof is unavailable)
blocks.body:
# find the PID holding 8080, then suspend it with pssuspend (Sysinternals)
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8080 -State Listen | Select-Object OwningProcess
pssuspend <pid>          # resume later with: pssuspend -r <pid>

blocks.label: Watch ledger's thread count climb while account is frozen
Re-run the load test in this state and record the p99 again

check.expect: While account is frozen, ledger is slow or unresponsive — including on endpoints that have nothing to do with account. That is the cascade.

tasks.do: Add a timeout — the smallest change with the biggest effect
tasks.why: One bounded wait converts an outage into a set of fast failures. Measure it before adding anything cleverer.
tasks.how: Set the connect and read timeouts on the RestClient behind the generated client. Re-run the frozen-account load test. The p99 should collapse to roughly your read timeout, and ledger should stay responsive throughout. Stop and compare the two numbers before continuing — this comparison is the point of the step.

blocks.label: ledger: config/AccountClientConfig.java — replace the bean method
Re-run the frozen test and compare
blocks.body:
kill -STOP $(lsof -ti:8080)
hey -z 30s -c 50 -m POST -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"accountId":"11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111","wallets":["A-12"]}' \
  http://localhost:8081/api/v1/holds
kill -CONT $(lsof -ti:8080)

check.run: # compare p99 with and without the timeout
check.expect: From tens of seconds to roughly 800ms, and ledger stays up.

tasks.do: Add retries with Spring Framework 7's built-in @Retryable
tasks.why: Some failures are a blip. Retrying a blip is free; retrying a genuine outage makes it worse, so bound it.
tasks.how: Spring Framework 7 ships declarative retry in the core framework — no spring-retry dependency. Annotate the method, enable it once with @EnableResilientMethods. Two rules worth internalising: only retry things that are safe to repeat (a read like this one), and always cap the attempts and back off between them.

blocks.label: ledger: config/ResilienceConfig.java
ledger: wrap the call in a bean you can annotate
Point PlaceHold at the gateway instead of the raw client

tasks.do: Add a fallback so an account outage degrades instead of failing
tasks.why: A cached balance view is a much better answer than a 500, and it keeps ledger useful while account recovers.
tasks.how: Cache the last successful answer per account and serve it when every retry has failed. This is a deliberately simple in-memory cache — it is enough to demonstrate the shape, and step 13 builds the real read model. Decide consciously what is acceptable here: serving a stale balance view risks holding a wallet that was just deleted, which is usually preferable to refusing all business.

blocks.label: ledger: AccountGateway — add the cache and the recovery method
Optional: a real circuit breaker
blocks.body:
Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker (Resilience4j) is the usual next step, but as of
Spring Cloud 2025.1.x its Resilience4j binding is still catching up with Boot 4,
so check compatibility before adding it:

  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-circuitbreaker-resilience4j</artifactId>
  </dependency>

  <!-- root pom, dependencyManagement -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-dependencies</artifactId>
    <version>2025.1.2</version>
    <type>pom</type><scope>import</scope>
  </dependency>

If it is not yet usable, the timeout + bounded retry + fallback above already
give you most of the protection. The breaker adds one thing on top: it stops
calling a service that is clearly down, instead of paying the timeout every time.

tasks.do: Repeat the frozen-account test and write both numbers down
tasks.why: Two measured numbers are the deliverable of this step. Not the configuration — the evidence.
tasks.how: Same load, same freeze, same duration. Compare against the baseline you recorded at the start. Keep the numbers in a file in the repo; you will want them again in step 14 when you are building dashboards, and they are the most convincing thing you can show anyone about why these patterns exist.

blocks.label: docs/measurements/step-06-cascade.md
blocks.body:
mkdir -p docs/measurements && cat > docs/measurements/step-06-cascade.md << 'EOF'
# Step 06 - cascading failure, measured

| scenario                              | p99      | ledger responsive? |
|---------------------------------------|----------|-----------------------|
| both healthy                          |    ?? ms | yes                   |
| account frozen, no timeout            |    ?? s  | no                    |
| account frozen, 800ms timeout         |    ?? ms | yes                   |
| account frozen, timeout + fallback    |    ?? ms | yes, serving cached   |

What I learned:
EOF

proof.expect: Ledger keeps answering throughout, with a p99 near the timeout rather than near infinity.
proof.note: Without a timeout, threads pile up until ledger dies too. That cascade is the thing every later pattern is defending against.

doneWhen: Freezing account degrades ledger instead of taking it down, and you have written down the before and after numbers.

lessons.title: Debug instead of printing
lessons.teach: Click the gutter to set a breakpoint, then start with Debug. Right-click the breakpoint for a condition — that is how you stop on the one request out of a hundred that fails.
lessons.fallbackTip: Add logging and read the second exception, not the first.
